claim: Ko & Yang (2021), full text read locally (reports/research/iterations/h20260929_02_pre_holiday_etf/sources/ko-yang-2021-pre-holiday-premium-small-firm.txt). Replicate Ariel (1990) on CRSP EW/VW indices 1963-1982, then extend to 1983-2019 (296 pre-holidays, 9032 non-pre-holidays over 8 federal holidays). 1983-2019: mean pre-holiday return 0.37% (EW) / 0.14% (VW) vs a much smaller non-pre-holiday mean; VW t-stat for the difference falls from 7.03 (1963-1982) to 1.92 (1983-2019) and to 1.19/1.23 in the 1990-2019/1995-2019 subperiods -- 'the pre-holiday premium of the CRSP VW index completely vanished after 1990'. DJIA and S&P 500 (large-firm-only indices) 1983-2019 pre-holiday-vs-non t-stats are 0.64 and 0.93 (insignificant). EW-VW (small-minus-large) difference on pre-holidays is 0.07pp with t=2.32 in 1983-2019 -- 'small firms had higher pre-holiday premium than large firms after controlling for other calendar effects'.
quote: we find that the pre-holiday effect now exists only among small firms. For large firms, the differences in returns between pre-holidays and non-pre-holidays have become insignificant, and especially after 1990.
applicability: Primary source for this iteration's mechanism (small-cap-only survival of the pre-holiday premium) and for the magnitude check in report.md (expected single-day premium on the order of 0.1-0.4pp, only ~9-10 events/year -- sets the prior that annualized Sharpe from holding only around holidays is likely to be low even if the mean-return direction is confirmed).
limitations: Index-level (CRSP EW/VW, DJIA, S&P 500), not ETF-level; no direct SVXY/IWM/SPY-equivalent test. Pre-1983 vs sample-period definitions of 'small firm' are CRSP-decile based, not IWM/IJR/IWC/VB's actual index-tracked market-cap bands -- this iteration's ETF choice is a project-side proxy, not from the paper itself.
independent_replication: The paper itself is a replication-plus-extension of Ariel (1990); no third independent replication of Ko & Yang specifically was found or read this round.
impact_on_spec: Grounds the small-cap-vs-large-cap ticker split and the magnitude expectation used in direction-review.json's target_regime_and_horizon and stop_condition.

claim: Ariel, R.A. (1990), 'High Stock Returns before Holidays: Existence and Evidence on Possible Causes', Journal of Finance 45(5):1611-1626. CRSP EW/VW index returns on trading days before 8 US holidays (1963-1982) were 8.6x (EW) / 14.4x (VW) the average non-pre-holiday return, t-stats 9.12/7.03; the effect was independent of the small-firm effect in that original sample.
quote: the average returns of pre-holidays and non-pre-holidays from 1963 to 1982 are 0.49% and 0.06% for the CRSP EW index, and 0.37% and 0.03% for the CRSP VW index
applicability: Original claim this iteration and Ko & Yang (2021) both test; establishes the pre-holiday-day definition (last trading day before one of 8 federal-market holidays) this batch's calendar rule reproduces via a gap-in-trading-days check.
limitations: Not independently re-fetched this round -- cited via Ko & Yang (2021)'s own replication and quotation of its numbers, not read from the original 1990 Journal of Finance article directly.
independent_replication: Ko & Yang (2021) is itself the independent out-of-sample replication of this claim (see ko_yang_2021_pre_holiday_small_firm_replication).
impact_on_spec: Defines the pre-holiday formation-date convention used by scripts/screen_batches/h20260929_02_pre_holiday_etf.py.

claim: Kim and Park (1994) extended Ariel's (1990) analysis to NYSE, AMEX, NASDAQ, the UK and Japan and found the pre-holiday effect present in all of these markets; they also found the small-firm effect was not present on pre-holidays in that (1963-1982-era) sample -- consistent with Ariel's own original finding that the effect was independent of firm size at the time.
quote: Kim and Park (1994) extended Ariel's (1990) analyses to three major stock exchanges in the U.S. (NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ), the U.K., and Japan and showed that the pre-holiday effect was present in these markets, too. They further showed that the small-firm effect was not present on pre-holidays.
applicability: Background: confirms the pre-holiday effect's cross-market robustness historically, but at a time (pre-1994) when it had not yet concentrated in small firms -- corroborates Ko & Yang's framing that the small-firm concentration is itself a later, decay-driven development, not present from the start.
limitations: Not independently re-fetched this round -- cited via Ko & Yang (2021)'s own literature review, not read directly.
impact_on_spec: Context only; does not set a manifest parameter.

claim: McLean and Pontiff (2016) find that the return predictability of published asset-pricing anomalies declines substantially after publication (out-of-sample and post-publication decay, attributed partly to statistical bias and partly to investors' learning/trading it away). Ko & Yang (2021) cite this as the general mechanism consistent with the pre-holiday premium's disappearance among large, liquid (easily arbitraged) firms while persisting among small, harder-to-arbitrage firms.
quote: The disappearance of the pre-holiday effect among large firms is in line with the observations of Schwert (2003) and McLean and Pontiff (2016) that the return predictability of asset-pricing anomalies declines substantially after their publications.
applicability: General mechanism grounding for why a large-cap ETF group (SPY, QQQ -- easy to arbitrage, high liquidity) is expected to show the effect 'largely gone' while a small/micro-cap ETF group (IWM/IJR/IWC/VB -- harder to arbitrage per-name, though the ETFs themselves are liquid) might retain more of it; also the source of this iteration's 'limits of arbitrage' framing for why any surviving small-cap-tier effect could plausibly still exist.
limitations: General anomaly-decay literature, not specific to the pre-holiday effect or to ETF-level (as opposed to individual-stock-level) arbitrage; not independently re-fetched this round.
impact_on_spec: Context only; does not set a manifest parameter.
